title: Best Gaming Mice UK
short: Wireless and wired gaming mice compared by weight, sensor and grip style, for FPS, MMO and all-round use.
intro: The right gaming mouse depends heavily on grip style and genre: FPS players usually want the lightest, simplest mouse possible, while MMO players want buttons within reach of every finger. This guide compares mice tested by Tom's Hardware, which says it has tested hundreds of gaming mice, across budget, wireless, compact and specialist picks.

products.name: G Pro X Superlight 2 SE
products.best_for: Competitive FPS players who want the lightest, simplest mouse possible
products.key_spec: 60g, Hero 2 sensor, 32,000 DPI, up to 2,000Hz polling
products.summary: Tom's Hardware's best FPS pick. The SE is a special-edition colourway of the standard Superlight 2, which the reviewer found very light, comfortable across multiple grip types, and smooth, speedy and low-latency, upgrading the original Superlight with USB-C charging, a faster Hero 2 sensor and 95 hours of battery life, about 35% more than its predecessor.
cons: No DPI switch on the mouse itself
products.search: Logitech G Pro X Superlight 2 SE gaming mouse

products.name: Basilisk V3 Pro 35K
products.best_for: Buyers who want one all-purpose mouse for any genre
products.summary: A comfortable, ergonomic all-purpose mouse with 11 programmable buttons and bright customisable RGB, hitting a sweet spot between performance, comfort and looks, though it's heavy and expensive for what's fundamentally an update to the previous model.
pros: New sensor and better battery life
Predecessor now cheaper as an alternative
cons: Broadly the same as the previous model
products.search: Razer Basilisk V3 Pro 35K gaming mouse

products.name: DeathAdder V4 Pro
products.best_for: Buyers who want a stripped-down, ultra-comfortable shape
products.key_spec: 56g, Focus Pro 45K sensor, up to 150hr battery
products.summary: Tom's Hardware calls this the best mouse shape it has tested. It's 10% lighter than its predecessor with a better sensor, switches, scroll wheel and battery life, though it doesn't have Bluetooth or RGB, and it's expensive for a simple mouse.
cons: Only a modest upgrade over the V3 Pro
products.search: Razer DeathAdder V4 Pro gaming mouse

products.name: Katar Pro XT
products.best_for: Buyers who want a comfortable, reliable mouse on a tight budget
products.summary: A lightweight, comfortable, ambidextrous budget mouse that doesn't feel cheap, with a paracord cable that glides without drag, though the wireless version often costs barely more.
cons: Wireless version often costs about the same
Not as light as pricier alternatives
products.search: Corsair Katar Pro XT gaming mouse

products.name: M686 Vampire Elite
products.best_for: Budget buyers who want wireless with a good feature set
products.summary: A well-built budget wireless mouse with grooves for the ring and pinky fingers, USB-C charging and 8 programmable buttons, though the scroll wheel feels imprecise and the software is close to mandatory to reprogram default button assignments.
pros: Unique ring and pinky finger grooves
Strong feature set for the price
cons: Side buttons oddly programmed out of the box
products.search: Redragon M686 Vampire Elite gaming mouse

products.name: G502 X Plus
products.best_for: Buyers who want striking lighting and lots of buttons
products.summary: Tom's Hardware calls its RGB lighting among the prettiest it has seen on a mouse, with 13 programmable buttons and hybrid optical-mechanical switches, though it's expensive, large, and the scroll wheel can feel twitchy.
products.search: Logitech G502 X Plus gaming mouse

products.name: G Pro Wireless
products.best_for: Left-handed players, or anyone who wants true symmetry
products.summary: One of the few truly ambidextrous gaming mice, with thumb buttons on both sides, a light matte shell, and claimed battery life of up to 60 hours, though Tom's Hardware noted some users report accidental double-clicks developing after around two years of use.
pros: Comfortable for left and right hands
Removable left and right side buttons
products.search: Logitech G Pro Wireless gaming mouse

products.name: Cobra Pro
products.best_for: Smaller hands who still want flagship-level features
products.key_spec: 77g, Focus Pro 30K sensor, up to 170hr battery over Bluetooth
products.summary: A smaller, lighter mouse than most flagships, without stripping out RGB or features, well suited to smaller hands, though Tom's Hardware felt it's too small for some and has fewer buttons than rivals.

products.name: Naga V2 Pro
products.best_for: MMO and MOBA players who want many programmable buttons
products.key_spec: 134g, swappable side plates, up to 20 buttons
products.summary: A versatile MMO mouse with three swappable side plates (2, 6 or 12 buttons) and a uniquely customisable scroll wheel that lets you tweak tension, steps and haptic feel, though it's heavy and very expensive.

guide.q: How light a mouse do I actually need?
guide.a: Competitive FPS players tend to favour the lightest mice available, often under 65g, for fast, low-fatigue flicks. For general gaming, MMO or productivity use, a heavier mouse (80-130g) with more buttons is often more comfortable and practical.

Maximum DPI figures are largely a marketing number, since most players use well under 5,000 DPI in practice. Sensor accuracy, consistent tracking and low latency matter far more to actual performance than the maximum DPI on the box.

Polling rate is how often the mouse reports its position to your PC, measured in Hz. A standard 1,000Hz polling rate is enough for the vast majority of players; higher rates like 2,000-8,000Hz mainly benefit top-level competitive players and often need a specific wireless dongle to unlock.

guide.q: Wireless or wired for competitive gaming?
guide.a: Modern wireless gaming mice, like several here, offer latency that's indistinguishable from wired for practical purposes, while removing cable drag entirely. Wired remains a safe, cheaper option if you'd rather not think about charging a mouse.
